s01.slug: TUESDAY · 3:20 AM · DELGADO HALL, UNDER THE OVERHANG
body: The alarm comes into the dream as a goose, and then it’s the goose-horn in the ceiling of 412 and the strobe going white on the crucifix, and it’s three in the morning. Theo is already at the door in the navy silk robe with a golf umbrella under his arm and both bags off the top shelf of the closet, the gray and the black. Jack gets the Carhartt off the hook and his feet into his shoes without socks and follows him down four flights of people swearing.

Outside, the storm has come in the dark. Not rain yet, mostly: wind, straight off the Lagoon and hard enough to lean on, and the eucalyptus behind Anacapa thrashing over the roofline with the sound of surf in the wrong place, the menthol smell of them torn open and blowing everywhere. A branch the size of a canoe lies across the bike path. Then the rain, sideways, a bucketful at a time, out of a sky Jack can’t see.

Three hundred and ten people cannot stand on the Delgado lawn tonight, so they don’t. They jam in under the concrete overhang along the front of the building and under the carport of the Anacapa lot, in boxers and towels and comforters and a collective mood. Somebody has brought a pillow. Somebody has brought a girl from another dorm, and both of them would prefer that not be discussed.
Priya is out in the fire lane with the air horn in one hand and the other hand held high over her head, and in it, sealed in a gallon Ziploc against the weather, a laminate.

body.title: Laminated, in a Ziploc
body.text: STORM PROTOCOL · STAY UNDER THE OVERHANG · DO NOT STAND UNDER TREES · DO NOT GO BACK FOR LAPTOPS · —P. RAMAN, RA

body: Kevin is calling the roll off a clipboard he keeps zipped inside his quarter-zip between names. “If you can hear me, you’re alive,” he tells the fourth floor, “and if you’re alive, you’re accounted for. That’s just science.”

Margot is dry. There is no account for this. She stands at the dead center of the overhang in a black raincoat buttoned to the throat with the Moleskine open on her palm, and the rain, which has gotten everybody else, appears to have declined her. She checks her watch against the page. “Twenty-five,” she tells Jack. Eighteen days from the last one would have been last Tuesday, and last Tuesday the building slept like a baby. She looks out at the storm with professional disappointment. “Either he’s irregular,” she says, “or he’s two people.” She puts the Moleskine away in an inside pocket, where it stays dry too.

At the far end of the building the wrong fire door swings open and Doug Pruitt comes out of it into the weather, barefoot, his pillow under his arm, and walks straight through the ankle-deep puddle at the bottom of the steps without waking up, and finds the overhang by instinct.

Theo holds the golf umbrella over himself, the two bags and Laney, in that order of priority. Laney is wearing a Hefty bag. It’s a black contractor bag with a hole torn in it for her face, and she has put her pearls on over it.

And Lena is at the other end of the overhang. Alone, at the very edge, where the rain gets her every time it comes and she doesn’t move in out of it. She’s in a man’s green Tulane sweatshirt that can only be Wes’s, left behind or left on purpose: the hood up, the sleeves pulled down over her hands, the green gone soft and pale with washing and TULANE across the chest in a white that is mostly memory. The hem comes to mid-thigh, over sleep shorts, over the Justins, unlaced. Thirty dry people separate her from Laney, and the two of them are not speaking, and it is visible from space. Jack doesn’t know why, and no one’s said.

The last time he saw her was Monday morning in the Anacapa lot, with Wes’s duffel going into the back of the Odyssey. The last time he heard her was Monday night, two floors down the stairwell, on the phone, and he has had the sound of it in his ear since. She sees him. She pushes the hood back with the back of her wrist.
“Morning, Jack.”
Polite. The weekend is in it.

journal.title: The 3 a.m. alarm
journal.text: Alarm 1, Monday the 31st, 3:07: everybody on the lawn in what they sleep in; Theo saved the espresso machine; Margot wrote ‘ALARM 1’ like it was a case number. Alarm 2, Friday the 18th, 3:12: eighteen days. Margot says that’s not a schedule, it’s a person. She’s keeping a log. Tuesday the 6th, nothing. Either the theory’s wrong or he’s on vacation. Alarm 3, Tuesday the 13th, 3:20, in a storm, under the overhang: twenty-five days. Margot says he’s irregular or he’s two people.

choices.text: Go stand at her end of the overhang.
response: He goes down the overhang through thirty people and stands at the edge with her, where the rain gets him too. She lets him. She says nothing, and he says nothing back, and the rain has plenty to say on its own. When the all-clear goes at 3:41 she says, “Thank you,” to the lawn, and goes in first.

In the fourth-floor hall Laney falls in behind Theo and Jack with her pillow. “I’m seeking asylum.” Theo doesn’t break stride. “Granted.” The Aerobed comes back out of its box (“Still warm from a Cajun”), Theo trades her the navy silk for the black Meridian robe, and there’s whispering across the dark in a language that sounds like seating charts. By four Laney is asleep. Jack lies awake and listens to the rain.

choices.text: “Is this a Louisiana thing, standing in it?”
response: “We call it *Tuesday*.”
For a second it’s her real voice, the fast one with the river in it, and then it’s gone, and she’s looking at the parking lot.

choices.text: Leave her be. Go stand with Laney and Theo.
response: He ducks in under the golf umbrella. Laney turns in the bag to face him, at full pageant. “I’ve been *exiled*. From my own *room*. Over a *tin*.”
“She’s been exiled,” Theo says.
For the next eighteen minutes Laney does not look down the overhang at Lena once, conspicuously, with her whole body.

In the fourth-floor hall she falls in behind them with her pillow. “I’m seeking asylum.” Theo doesn’t break stride. “Granted.” The Aerobed comes back out of its box (“Still warm from a Cajun”), Theo trades her the navy silk for the black Meridian robe, and there’s whispering across the dark in a language that sounds like seating charts. s02.slug: TUESDAY · 3:50 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOBBY MAILBOXES
body: No mail Monday, for Columbus, so Tuesday there are two days of it, and at ten to four the Delgado lobby smells like wet wool and wet cardboard and two hundred people’s rain. What the alarm was announcing has arrived in full. It comes down the lobby glass in sheets so thick the fire lane is a rumor, and the palms out front are bent double, hunting for something they dropped. Marcus is asleep at the front desk with his mouth open over an orgo text, which is where Marcus has spent the semester.

*The Moviegoer* is in Jack’s back pocket, the Vintage paperback with its spine cracked white, out of the milk crate this morning because Binx Bolling is on a search and Jack has a paper due tomorrow at one about whether a man can know his own heart, and so far the paper is a title. Hale’s Williams is upstairs on the desk, where it has been reminding him all week of the margins he owes it.

His box has a Newman flyer, a credit card offer for JOHN COSTIGAN, and the envelope: block capitals, DANIEL F. COSTIGAN and the number after it, the return address printed by the institution, a Leavittsburg postmark from Friday. He opens it standing at the mailboxes.

body.title: TRUMBULL CORRECTIONAL INSTITUTION
body.text:
PROFESSOR,
The Hopkins came. Took me a week to get past the first one but then I got to Felix Randal, the horse guy, the blacksmith, and I read it to Ma on the phone Tuesday and she cried, so thanks for that, I’m telling you so you know I read it. Not so you feel bad.
The Housman came too. Tell your man who don’t sleep that nobody in here does either. Number LIV made Reggie cry and Reggie is from Portsmouth.
Ma says there’s a girl now. Becca. From Idaho. Ma says she’s a nice girl. Ma says it how she says the Browns got a nice stadium.
Did you tell Lena hey or do I got to come out there.
Reggie asked me do I ever wish I did it different. I told him I don’t wish. I decided. It’s different.
Push-ups 140. Browns are 0-4 so don’t call me about it.
—D.

body: Jack stands at the mailboxes with the letter open in his hands. Behind him the door lets in a gust and a girl with a broken umbrella, and the umbrella goes into the trash can by the desk with a sound like a bird hitting a window, and Marcus doesn’t wake up. The rain keeps coming down the glass. Jack stands there until the girl is gone and the lobby is just the rain again.

journal.title: Danny Costigan
journal.text: My brother. Trumbull Correctional. Calls me Professor. Ma brought him the good socks. *Brideshead* went to him through Driftwood, margins erased; the C.O. reading it first says it’s about a house. The ocean letter got there; Reggie, from Portsmouth, decided on his own the Pacific smells like money and fish. Lena knows. She asked his name. On the bluff bench she said hi to him and told him she’s going to be defense, and he laughed like he used to. The system cut him off at ‘tell Gina — .’ He wrote the rest down: tell Gina it ain’t hers to carry. He’s got it. On Michaelmas he wrote: Tell Lena hey. I like knowing it. You sound happy out there. Don’t feel bad about it. That’s an order. Lena says hey back. She said it herself. The Saints are four and oh, and she expects him to know that. Third letter, after Columbus Day: the Hopkins got there. He read Ma “Felix Randal” on the phone and she cried; he says he’s telling me so I know he read it, not so I feel bad. The Housman made Reggie cry. Ma told him about Becca. He wants to know if I told Lena hey, or does he have to come out here. I did. He doesn’t know yet. Push-ups: 140.

choices.text: Read it again, on the stairs.
response: He sits on the second-floor landing with the stairwell’s one window running like a gutter and goes through it again from PROFESSOR down. When he gets to the push-ups he laughs, once, out loud, alone, and it goes up the stairwell and comes back to him off the concrete.

Then the 11 bus, since La Flaca isn’t going anywhere in this. At 4:35, the post office on Mission, wet newsprint and a clerk who doesn’t look up: a $20.00 money order, $21.10 with the fee, PAY TO: D. KOSTELNIK, STRUTHERS, OH, the street from memory, FROM blank. It goes in the OUT OF TOWN slot. The stub goes behind his Mooney ID against the first one, and his right hand closes on it there before he puts the wallet away. Then the bus on to the harbor, for seven.

choices.text: Fold it into *The Moviegoer* and go.
response: It goes in between Binx and the search, and the book goes back in his pocket, and he goes.

response: He takes it up four flights to the desk and slides it into the Williams where his own pencil stops, a page short of Williams’s lorry driver, and comes back down two steps at a time.

body: The harbor is having the worst night of its year. The boats in the slips knock against the pilings without letup, the sea lions who bark under the docks every other night of the week have gone dead quiet, and the rain comes across the wharf in sheets and drums on the glass of the window booth, which is empty. They’re all empty. Tuesday is half-price chowder, and tonight it is half-price chowder for no one. Ray Ochoa’s stool, where the meatloaf goes on Tuesdays, is bare. Jack has run the Hobart three times since seven mostly to have something to do with his hands, and his share of the tip jar is shaping up to be a dime and a peppermint.

At a quarter past nine Gloria comes out from behind the register with the pencil through her gray bun and a quarter in her fingers, walks the length of the empty room to the jukebox, puts the quarter in, and plays Sinatra into a gale. She doesn’t explain it. She walks back to the register. On the shelf over the pass Rudy’s transistor has no Dodgers tonight, the Dodgers being off till Thursday and Philadelphia; it has KCBX instead, a man reading out wind speeds and running low on synonyms for *heavy*.

The only customers since eight are two women at the counter in Harbor Inn housekeeping smocks under their rain jackets, one in her fifties and one maybe twenty-five, waiting out a 7 bus that was supposed to come at eight, then at ten. Gloria has put soup and grilled cheese in front of them and written no ticket, and when the older one went for her purse Gloria looked at her until she stopped. The younger one is showing the older one pictures on a phone with a cracked face, a baby in a pumpkin hat, and the older one is unimpressed on principle.
Gloria fills their cups. “Dulce. Rosario. This one’s Jack. He knows your New Orleans girl.”

Jack, at the end of the counter with a bus tub on his hip, knows one New Orleans girl, and can’t think how she could be theirs. Rosario looks him over, apron to cowlick, and says something to Dulce in Spanish, quick, and Dulce laughs into her soup.

From the pass, without looking up from the flattop, Rudy translates. “They say your friend brings soup. Sundays. To the hotel, for the night girls.” Dulce adds something, pointing her spoon at Jack. “The New Orleans girl,” Rudy says. Dulce adds one more thing, and Rosario nods hard, agreeing. Rudy scrapes the grill. “They say it needs salt.”
Jack didn’t know. He thought he knew a fair amount about where Lena Broussard is on a given night of the week, and he didn’t know that.
At the end of the counter Gloria comes back with the pot and fills his coffee, which he did not ask for, and stands there with it.

body.text: “Saturday,” she says. “Merle. You got a laugh.”
body.else: “Saturday,” she says. “That fisherman. You kept your mouth shut.” She holds the pot. “Pie or the door, hon.”

response: “Lots of things work, hon.” She leaves it there and tops off his coffee.

At half past twelve she sends him home, and the last 11 comes at 12:40, late, through gutters running like creeks. Dulce and Rosario ride it too, the 7 never having come, and by Ocean Road they’re asleep against each other three seats up, and when it turns in past the Grove the eucalyptus are roaring in the dark outside the windows.
“No,” Gloria agrees, and tops it off anyway. “That’s why I brought it up.” Later, wiping down the counter by the pie case, not to him: “Lots of things work.”

At half past twelve she sends him home, and the last 11 comes at 12:40, late, through gutters running like creeks. Dulce and Rosario ride it too, the 7 never having come, and by Ocean Road they’re asleep against each other three seats up, and when it turns in past the Grove the eucalyptus are roaring in the dark outside the windows.
She waits him out with the pot in her hand, a contest with no winner in it, and then: “Lots of things work, hon.”

Dulce and Rosario ride it too, the 7 never having come, and by Ocean Road they’re asleep against each other three seats up, and when it turns in past the Grove the eucalyptus are roaring in the dark outside the windows.

s04.slug: WEDNESDAY · 1:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE BASEMENT LAUNDRY
body: The walk from the bus stop on Ocean Road was four hundred yards of horizontal water, and Jack owns one pair of jeans, so at twenty to two in the morning he goes down to the basement in gym shorts with the jeans in a wet wad under his arm to put them in a dryer and stand in front of it.

The laundry room is warm and smells the way it always smells, sweet and chemical, dryer sheets and lint and somebody’s abandoned towels going sour in a washer. Eight washers. Six dryers, three of them dark tonight and three tumbling. Against the far wall, the old upright piano with its lid down, the one with the dead F.

Priya is sitting on the floor by the door at the back marked RA STORAGE — NOT A STUDY ROOM, in Facilities stencil, black. She has the hood of her Fremont High sweatshirt up and a Ziploc of orgo flashcards on her knees, and she has packed every towel in the laundry room along the bottom of the door in a dam, including several that are not hers. Water is coming under it anyway. A dark tongue of it has gotten past the towels and is spreading across the linoleum toward the dryers.
“The laundry room closes at eleven,” she says, without looking up.
“You’re here.”

“I’m *staff*.” She turns a flashcard over, reads it, turns it back. “I have orgo at eight a.m. It’s warm down here, the dryers, 401 is a refrigerator. I have my library shift tomorrow night, midnight to eight. And I have a *lake* in my *closet*.”

She stands up with a ring of keys, forty of them, color-coded with nail polish, and finds the purple one on the third try. The door opens inward on two inches of storm water, brown, come in through the window well and lying flat and still over the whole floor of the closet. Holiday decorations in a box marked DECEMBER. A carton of confiscated candles, labeled. Last year’s lost-and-found in a black garbage bag slumped against the wall. And on the floor at the back, in the water, a banker’s box with a Sharpie label: CALLOWAY · 222 · HOLD FOR FAMILY. HOLD is underlined twice. The bottom corner of the box has gone dark and soft.
Jack knows the name. Priya told it to him over a grocery cupcake at about this hour of a Wednesday, five weeks ago.

They lift it out together, careful of the soft corner, and set it on top of a working dryer, which is warm. Priya opens the lid to check the damage. A gray sweatshirt that says SELMA HIGH. CDs in a zip case. A mug. A photo of two girls laughing in a dorm window with the blinds pulled up crooked, and one of them is Priya, with bangs. A black-and-white composition book, the bottom edge of it wet and ruffling. Priya picks that up last and opens the cover. Only the cover.

body.title: Inside the cover
body.text: Nora Calloway · Delgado 222 · If found, please return. Reward: I’ll sing you something.

body: She closes it. “I’ve never gotten past this page.” She sets it back on top of the sweatshirt and squares it with the edge of the box, twice. The Calloways never came for it. She can’t throw it out, and she can’t mail it. “You can’t mail somebody their daughter’s *mug*.”

Then she breaks, completely and at speed. “I *tutor* organic chemistry. I’m *failing* organic chemistry. My parents think I’m going to be a doctor. They run a *motel*.” She sits down on the dryer beside the box with her flashcards in her lap and cries hard, for about forty seconds, with her mouth open, and the dryer goes on tumbling under her. Then she wipes her face on her Fremont High sleeve, both sides, and says, “Okay,” and goes upstairs, and comes back down with the laminator from 401.

At 2:20 in the morning it is plugged in beside the dryers, warming up with its little orange light, and Priya is writing on a sheet of printer paper in block capitals with a Sharpie, and then the sheet goes through, and comes out the other side hot and sealed and permanent. She tapes it to the front of the dryers, corners first.

body.title: Taped to the dryers
body.text: BASEMENT FLOODED · DRYERS 1–3 ONLY · DO NOT OPEN RA STORAGE · —P. RAMAN, RA

body: Jack’s jeans have been dry for ten minutes.

journal.title: Hold for family
journal.text: A banker’s box in the RA storage closet, three-quarters of a year: CALLOWAY · 222 · HOLD FOR FAMILY. HOLD underlined twice. A Selma High sweatshirt, CDs, a mug, a picture of two girls laughing in a dorm window — one of them Priya. A composition book. Inside the cover: Nora Calloway · Delgado 222 · If found, please return. Reward: I’ll sing you something. Priya has never gotten past that page. Nobody came for it. It lives in 401 now.

journal.title: Nora Calloway
journal.text: The name on the plaque. Priya’s freshman roommate, Delgado 222. From Selma — raisins. Sang soprano; sang the Memorare in the shower. Philosophy. Fell at the Point at the end of April. Tuesday would have been her twentieth birthday. Facebook won’t stop suggesting her. Her things are in a box in Priya’s room now. On the inside cover of her journal she promised whoever found it a song.

journal.title: Priya (RA)
journal.text: Laminates things. Owns an air horn. Her freshman roommate was Nora Calloway. The one rule she doesn’t laminate is for her. Three jobs: RA, the library overnight desk, orgo tutor. Failing orgo, she says. Her parents run a motel in Fremont and think she’s going to be a doctor. Re-laminated the laundry room at two in the morning.

choices.text: “You don’t have to open it. Not ever.”
choices.key: In the flooded basement you helped Priya carry Nora’s box upstairs. She wouldn’t open the journal past the first page.
response: She looks at him as if he’s said something illegal. Then she nods twice, fast, the way she does at the bottom of a laminate.

They take it up the east stairs together, four flights, because Priya doesn’t trust the elevator with anything wet, her walking backward with the soft corner and the laminator riding on the lid. In 401 it goes on the floor under her window beside the mini-fridge and the place the laminator lives, and it lives there now too. At the door she says, “Good luck on your thing,” because she knows everybody’s midterm schedule, and he’s halfway down the hall before he works out that she means Thursday.

body: Five past three, and the rain is still coming at the window in long rattling handfuls. On a clear night the old light on the Point shows from here, dark on dark past the Grove. Tonight there’s only the water on the glass.

Laney is asleep on the Aerobed in Theo’s navy silk, flat on her back with her hands folded on her stomach, snoring delicately through her nose, a lady about it even unconscious. Theo is at his desk in the dark with his headphones on and the MacBook lit, some French film going in black and white with the subtitles crawling, and he isn’t watching it. He’s looking at the window.
Jack sits up on his bed with the yellow legal pad on his knee. At the top of it, underlined, in his own hand since Monday night: *That a Man Can Know His Own Heart.* Under that, two days of nothing.

body.text: Danny’s letter is in *The Moviegoer* on the desk, folded between Binx and the search.
Danny’s letter is in the Williams on the desk, where his pencil stops.
Danny’s letter is on the desk, unfolded flat under the lamp.

body: He writes the first sentence.
*A man knows his own heart by what he says yes to.*

Then the rest comes, faster than his hand. Aristotle, *Ethics* II: we become just by doing just things, brave by doing brave ones, and the knowing comes after the doing, not before. James 2:18, *I by my works will show you my faith.* Binx Bolling on his search, who can’t find himself by looking and finds out who he is by what he does on a Wednesday. And Augustine, who is supposed to be her side of this: for a man who said he couldn’t know his own heart, he filled ten books with it. Jack fills two pages of the pad and turns it over and keeps going. He doesn’t look at the letter. He has Percy open on the blanket, spine up, and the pen going, and across the room the French film plays on in Theo’s headphones, small and tinny, and the rain keeps on at the window, and so does the pen.
